text:
sam: FYI customer A reported a big TTFB spike only on streaming responses (SSE) starting ~2024-06-08. Non-streaming (sync) endpoints unaffected. p95 up from 120ms -> 850ms, p99 ~2.3s.

maria: got the escalation — they sent traces and a reproducible curl script. They're hitting our edge via an ISP that proxies with HTTP/1.1.

zach: can you paste the curl we should run? I'll try to repro from our lab in us-west.

maria: sure:
```bash
# SSE streaming repro (http/1.1 fallback)
curl -sv -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \n  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \n  https://api.redwood.example/v1/streams/generate\n```

# sync request for comparison
```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \n  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n  -d '{"prompt":"hello","max_tokens":64}' \n  https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate
```

ingrid: repro'd it from a VM on the same peering as the customer. SSE first byte delayed ~700-900ms vs sync ~90-140ms. Total completion similar after streaming starts. Observed chunk coalescing on the edge: first chunk held until ~800B or 300ms.

edge-eng: that sounds like the edge proxy's coalescing window + Nagle on the upstream conn. We have a 250ms flush window and a 1KB coalesce target on that region. If client path forces h1 keepalive, it tends to combine.

sam: customer path uses legacy ISP that downgrades to http/1.1. They see p99 spikes tied to first-chunk delay. Any quick mitigations?

zach: options: 1) make streaming fallback to sync for that tenant (fast to flip but loses streaming UX), 2) set a header to force immediate flush on the edge for streaming requests, 3) adjust edge coalesce window for the region (requires rollout).

maria: customer asked for repro steps so we produced a small harness: run the curl SSE command 30x and log time to first byte and total. Attached logs show first-byte histogram: 20% <200ms, 60% 200-800ms, 20% >800ms.

ops-bot: deploy request created for a canary patch to add header-based flush bypass (PR #4281). Link: https://git.internal/pulls/4281

ingrid: small log excerpt from edge (redacted):
```
[edge-conn 12:14:05] accept from 1.2.3.4 method=GET path=/v1/streams/generate proto=HTTP/1.1
[buffer] accumulated=912B latency=312ms flush_reason=coalesce_size
[backend] recv first_kv=3ms backend_latency=45ms
[edge-send] first_byte_sent=780ms
```

zach: backend is fast — this confirms the edge is holding the first chunk. We can shorten the coalesce_size from 1KB to 128B for the affected region as a targeted mitigation. Will need config rollout and monitor.

sam: timeline proposals: immediate action: flip tenant to sync fallback (manual toggle) while we canary header bypass; short-term: canary header bypass to skip coalesce on matching header; medium: edge config change for region; long-term: expose a per-tenant streaming-flush policy.

maria: customer accepted temporary sync fallback (they prioritized deterministic latency over streaming). I've applied the toggle and asked them to re-run harness. They reported p95 back to ~140ms.

edge-eng: starting canary rollout for header bypass in eu-edge-03 (10% traffic) and will monitor first-byte histograms.

ops-bot: canary deployed: rolls/4281 -> eu-edge-03 (10%) at 2024-06-09T18:33:00Z

ingrid: after canary, SSE first-byte p95 dropped to ~230ms on canary nodes, p99 ~420ms. Non-canary still high.

zach: sounds promising. Plan to expand to 50% if no regressions in 30m. Also need an alert tweak so we distinguish streaming-first-byte regressions from total-latency regressions. Current SLOs aggregate both which hides streaming-specific regressions.

sam: filing follow-up: create a runbook for streaming TTFB where customer path uses http/1.1. Add checklist: reproduce harness, apply tenant sync fallback, canary header bypass, adjust edge coalesce_size, and postmortem if we change default coalescing.

maria: noted. I'll also loop in billing if this tenant requests a credit. For now they're happy with the fallback.

edge-eng: one engineering note — header bypass should be conservative: only for requests with Accept: text/event-stream and a per-tenant opt-in header to avoid increasing small-payload overhead everywhere.

sam: thanks all. If anyone finds additional ISPs with the same path behavior, drop the traceroute + curl results here and we'll add to the list. :thumbsup:
